text: Every image Northbridge has pulled so far -- node, ubuntu, postgres -- came from the same place: Docker Hub, the default public registry. This lesson flips the direction: pushing Northbridge's own image instead of just pulling other people's.

That's hub dot docker dot com itself -- the registry quietly behind every pull in this course. A registry is just a server that stores and serves images; Docker Hub is the default one, and a free account is all it takes to start pushing your own.

docker login authenticates the CLI, storing a token so later push and pull commands don't ask again. But a local image isn't connected to Hub until it's tagged with your namespace -- docker tag northbridge slash catalog colon 1.4 northbridgeretail slash catalog colon 1.4 -- then docker push actually uploads it. From here, anyone with access can pull that exact image.

Creating a repository on Docker Hub comes down to one real decision: visibility. Public repositories show up in search and anyone can pull them -- fine for open-source images. Private repositories are invisible in search and locked to accounts you've explicitly granted access.

Northbridge keeps northbridgeretail slash catalog and northbridgeretail slash checkout private -- they're the company's actual application code, not something meant for the public internet. A free Docker Hub account includes a limited number of private repositories; Northbridge pays for more as that number grows.

That image got pushed with tag 1.4 almost as an afterthought. Next lesson turns tagging into an actual strategy -- semantic versions, latest, and git-sha tags, and why some of them should never be overwritten.
